# Development of an Interactive Machine Learning-Based System for Next-Day PM2.5 Air Pollution Forecasting Using OpenWeatherMap API

*Course AMO 3208 Machine Learning Algorithms — Final Project (team of three). Draft generated by
`python -m air_quality.cli report` from the project's actual artifacts; every number below is read from
`artifacts/`. Team members: [Member 1 name], [Member 2 name], [Member 3 name].*

---

## Abstract

Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is the air pollutant most strongly linked to adverse health outcomes, and
Astana experiences pronounced winter pollution during the heating season. This project develops and evaluates a
reproducible machine learning (ML) system that forecasts the mean PM2.5 concentration of the next local calendar
day for Astana, Kazakhstan, using historical hourly data from the OpenWeatherMap Air Pollution API. Forecasts are
issued at 18:00 local time and use only information available at that moment. The dataset contains
43,273 hourly records (2020-12-26T00:00 to 2025-12-31T23:00 (local); timestamp coverage 98.42%). After cleaning and target
construction, train 1061, validation 351, test 346 eligible daily samples were obtained, with chronological train (2021–2023),
validation (2024) and independent test (2025) years. Four regression algorithms — Ridge Regression, Random
Forest, XGBoost and Support Vector Regression — and their equal-weight ensemble were tuned with time-series
cross-validation and compared with a persistence baseline across pollution-history feature configurations, a
feature-selection variant and configurations that add Open-Meteo meteorological information. The
model selected on validation data, Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) (full_weather features), obtained an independent 2025 test MAE
of 3.02 µg/m³ (RMSE 4.65 µg/m³, R² 0.414) compared with an MAE of
3.52 µg/m³ for persistence (+14.2% change in MAE). The system includes a command-line
application that produces a live next-day forecast from the latest API data.

**Keywords:** PM2.5; day-ahead forecasting; OpenWeatherMap; Random Forest; XGBoost; SVR; Ridge; persistence; Astana.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Background: air pollution and PM2.5

PM2.5 penetrates deep into the respiratory system, and the World Health Organization (2021) set its 24-hour
guideline level at 15 µg/m³. Short-term forecasts allow residents, schools and health services to plan around
high-pollution days.

### 1.2. Research problem and justification for Astana

Astana has a sharply continental climate with long, cold winters and a heating season of roughly six months.
Local research has linked PM2.5 exposure in Astana to a substantial health burden and found clear differences
between heating and non-heating periods (Agibayeva et al., 2022). Yet the verified Kazakh ML studies either
estimate concentrations from concurrent measurements (Agibayeva et al., 2022) or nowcast 15 minutes ahead
(Sapakova et al., 2026). A transparent, leakage-free **day-ahead** forecasting benchmark is missing.

### 1.3. Object, subject and methods of research

*Object:* PM2.5 concentrations for Astana as provided by the OpenWeatherMap Air Pollution API.
*Subject:* supervised regression methods for next-day mean PM2.5.
*Methods:* API data acquisition and validation, exploratory statistics, issue-time feature engineering,
regularized linear regression, tree ensembles, kernel regression, chronological validation, permutation
importance.

### 1.4. Aim

Develop and evaluate a reproducible machine learning system capable of predicting next-day PM2.5 concentration
in Astana using historical air pollution information.

### 1.5. Objectives

RO1 Collect and validate reliable historical air-pollution data from OpenWeatherMap. RO2 Analyse temporal
patterns, seasonality, correlations, missingness and pollutant distributions. RO3 Develop a leakage-free feature
engineering and preprocessing pipeline. RO4 Implement and optimise four regression algorithms. RO5 Compare the
models against each other and a persistence baseline using independent chronological testing. RO6 Analyse
feature importance, prediction errors and limitations. RO7 Demonstrate an actual next-day prediction through an
executable Python command. RO8 Document the methodology and connect findings to recent literature.

### 1.6. Research questions and hypotheses

RQ1 Which model provides the lowest next-day error? (H1: a tree ensemble.) RQ2 Do engineered historical features
improve on basic features? (H2: yes.) RQ3 Does ML outperform persistence? (H3: yes, skill > 0.) RQ4 Which
pollutants and temporal features contribute most? (H4: recent PM2.5 history.) RQ5 How robust are models on
elevated-PM2.5 days? (H5: errors are substantially larger and negatively biased.) Hypotheses are evaluated in
Section 4.8 from the measured results.

### 1.7. Theoretical and methodological basis; expected contribution

The work builds on regularized least squares (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970), bagged regression trees (Breiman, 2001),
regularized gradient boosting (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) and ε-insensitive support vector regression (Smola &
Schölkopf, 2004), evaluated with the chronological protocols recommended by recent forecasting benchmarks
(Psomadakis et al., 2026; Hyso & Gjylapi, 2026). The contribution is a documented, reproducible day-ahead
benchmark for Astana with an explicit persistence reference, and an operational command-line forecaster whose
architecture allows a graphical interface to be added later.

## 2. Literature Review

## 2.0. How the review was conducted and how to verify it

**Goal of the review.** Identify which machine learning models perform best in studies that are *similar to
ours* — daily or day-ahead PM2.5 forecasting from historical air-pollution data — and use that evidence to
choose the models we train.

**Selection.** Sixteen candidate studies (2022–2026) were screened; eleven were included after their
metadata and results were checked against the publisher page or an official repository (last verified
17 November 2026). Two candidates could not be retrieved and are not cited (see `literature_comparison.md`).

**How to verify a number yourself.** Every result below has a **"Where to look"** line giving the section,
table, figure or page of the original article. Open the DOI link from the reference list and go to that place.
Some MDPI and PMC tables are images on the web page; in that case the numbers are also stated in the article
text at the location given, or the PDF version shows the table.

**Two kinds of studies.** This distinction decides whether a result is comparable with ours:

* **Forecasting studies** predict PM2.5 for a *future* time using only past data (like our project).
* **Estimation studies** predict PM2.5 at the *same* time from simultaneously measured variables
  (co-pollutants, weather, satellite data). They usually report much higher accuracy, but they answer a
  different question and cannot be used directly for next-day forecasting.

---

## 2.1. Air pollution and PM2.5 forecasting

PM2.5 is the pollutant most closely linked to the health burden of urban air pollution; the World Health
Organization (2021) set its 24-hour guideline level at 15 µg/m³. In Astana, Agibayeva et al. (2022) estimated
that PM2.5 exposure in 2019 corresponded to roughly 2,160–7,531 disability-adjusted life years and found
clear differences between the heating (October–April) and non-heating periods
(*Where to look:* Section 3.7 and Tables 8 and 10 for DALY; Conclusions for the 2,160–7,531 range).

Three findings recur across the reviewed forecasting studies:

1. **PM2.5 is strongly persistent**, so simple "repeat the recent value" forecasts are hard to beat at short
   horizons (Sapakova et al., 2026).
2. **Accuracy drops quickly with the horizon**: XGBoost reached R² = 0.862 one hour ahead but R² = 0.50 at
   24 hours (Fetahi et al., 2025).
3. **Pollution episodes are the hardest to predict** (Haseeb et al., 2026; Agibayeva et al., 2022).

---

## 2.2. Study-by-study results

### A. Forecasting studies (past data → future PM2.5) — most relevant to us

**[L1] Sapakova et al. (2026), Almaty, Kazakhstan — *Technologies* 14(8), 512.**
*Data:* OpenWeather Air Pollution API (the same provider as ours), 5 virtual stations, 18 summer days in 2026,
modelled at 15/30/60-minute steps. *Task:* one-step-ahead nowcasting. *Models:* lag-1 persistence, Linear
Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting; chronological 80/20 split.
*Result:* at 15 minutes persistence had R² = 0.980, while the ML models reached 0.962–0.977; at 60 minutes
all ML models fell to R² ≤ 0.319 against 0.743 for persistence. In Random Forest, the current PM2.5 value
(≈0.72) and its 3-step rolling mean (≈0.24) dominated feature importance.
*Where to look:* Section 3.5 "PM2.5 Forecasting Results", Table 7 (results across 15/30/60 min) and
Figure 9 (Random Forest feature importance). MAE/RMSE values are only in Table 7.
*Meaning for us:* persistence must be included as a baseline; recent PM2.5 and rolling means are the key
features. Not directly comparable: 15-minute horizon, summer only.

**[L3] Fetahi et al. (2025), Prishtina, Kosovo — *Ecological Engineering & Environmental Technology* 26(8), 97–114.**
*Data:* hourly pollution, 2018–2024. *Task:* multi-horizon forecasting. *Models:* XGBoost, LightGBM, Random
Forest, SVM, Linear Regression; lag, rolling and cyclical time features; SHAP.
*Result:* **XGBoost was best**: R² = 0.862, MAE = 3.524, RMSE = 6.513 one hour ahead, and R² = 0.50 at the
24-hour horizon.
*Where to look:* the **Abstract** (all four numbers and the list of five models). Full PDF on the journal page
("Article (PDF)").
*Meaning for us:* the same model families we use; shows the expected accuracy loss at a 24-hour horizon.

**[L4] Psomadakis et al. (2026), Greece — *Electronics* 15(19), 4496.**
*Data:* open data from 5 Greek stations, daily means. *Task:* **next-day** PM2.5/PM10 and next-week maximum.
*Models:* Random Forest, **SVM (RBF)**, neural network, LSTM; persistence and SARIMA baselines.
*Design:* chronological boundaries fixed before gap-filling (Section 4.2); 40 sliding windows for model
selection plus a final 20% held-out set (Section 4.4); persistence baseline defined in Section 4.4.1.
*Result:* **SVM was the most broadly reliable model**, winning 13 of 20 combinations under held-out assessment
and 11 of 20 under model selection. On the held-out data **every ML model beat persistence at every station**
for next-day PM2.5, while SARIMA was worse than persistence at four of five stations. Example: SVM reached
R² = 0.458 at Volos-1.
*Where to look:* Abstract and Section 8 (Conclusions) for 13/20 and 11/20; Section 6.1 and **Table 8** (mean
R² for next-day PM2.5; best model in bold) and **Figure 9** (held-out R² by station and model); Section 6.3 for
the Volos-1 value; Section 7.6.3 for SARIMA vs persistence.
*Meaning for us:* the closest design to ours (next-day daily target, past-only features, persistence
baseline) and the main evidence for including **SVR**.

**[L5] Chivukula et al. (2026), nine U.S. cities — *Atmosphere* 17(8), 779.**
*Data:* EPA regulatory monitors, PurpleAir sensors and satellite PM2.5, 1998–2023. *Task:* **next-day daily
PM2.5**. *Design:* train 1998–2021, validation 2022, test 2023 — the same year-based design as ours.
*Result:* for the Dallas 2023 hold-out, **XGBoost had the highest R² (0.667)**, ahead of Random Forest
(0.588), Gradient Boosting (0.572) and the fused LSTM (0.555).
*Where to look:* Section 3.6, subsection "Baseline Model Comparisons", **Table 6** ("Baseline model
comparison for Dallas, TX, 2023 temporal holdout"); split years in **Table 4** (Section 3.3) and Section 3.5.
*Meaning for us:* on daily data, tree boosting beat deep learning; supports **XGBoost** and **Random Forest**
and our year-based split.

**[L6] Hyso & Gjylapi (2026), eight Albanian cities — *Baltic Journal of Modern Computing* 14(3), 618–644.**
*Data:* Open-Meteo/CAMS modelled air-quality fields (an open API product, like ours), 2024–2026. *Task:*
**1-, 2- and 3-day-ahead** daily mean PM2.5. *Models:* naive, seasonal naive, drift, Holt, ARIMA, Random
Forest (local baselines); persistence, **Ridge** and HistGradientBoosting with global features; XGBoost as a
challenger. *Design:* rolling-origin backtesting.
*Result:* for 1-day PM2.5 the best enhanced model (HistGBM) had **MAE = 1.92** versus **2.04** for the best
baseline (Random Forest with 7 lags); sMAPE 17.40% vs 18.15%. After Bonferroni adjustment none of the six main
improvements was clearly significant.
*Where to look:* **Table 4, page 631** (MAE comparison); Section 5.2, page 632 (sMAPE and significance);
Section 4.1, pp. 623–624 (rolling-origin design); Section 4.4, pp. 625–626 (Bonferroni analysis); Sections
4.2–4.3 (models); Section 4.7 and Tables 9–10 (XGBoost).
*Meaning for us:* the most similar data product and horizon; gains of ML over strong baselines are real but
small. Supports **Ridge** and **gradient boosting**.

**[L7] Abuouelezz et al. (2025), Abu Dhabi, UAE — *Scientific Reports* 15, 9797.**
*Data:* 6 monitoring stations, hourly, 2018–2022; split 80% training (4 years) / 20% testing (1 year).
*Task:* forecasting at 1 h, 2 h, 1 day and 1 week. *Models:* Decision Tree, Random Forest, linear SVR, RBF
SVR, 1D-CNN, LSTM, Prophet.
*Result:* **linear SVR was best for PM2.5 one hour ahead** (average over stations: MAE = 6.630,
RMSE = 15.911, MAPE = 0.187, i.e. 18.7%).
*Where to look:* **Table 5** (PM2.5 results by horizon and model; best values in bold, last row = average
across stations); "Data preprocessing" subsection of the Methodology for the 80/20 split. The 1-day values
are in the same table (the web version is hard to read; use the PDF).
*Meaning for us:* another study where **SVR** wins; shows the drop in accuracy towards a 1-day horizon.

**[L8] Bhatta, Acharya & Yang (2026), Bangkok, Thailand — *Environmental Challenges* 22, 101442.**
*Data:* 12 stations, 1,827 daily observations, 2020–2024, with meteorology. *Models:* Random Forest,
Gradient Boosting, LSTM; temporal lags, moving averages and cyclical encoding.
*Result:* **Gradient Boosting performed best** (RMSE = 2.17 µg/m³); regularization limited the drop from
training to external validation to 3.9% (GB) and 5.6% (RF).
*Where to look:* **Abstract** (Macquarie University and Mahidol University repository records; full text via
the DOI).
*Meaning for us:* daily PM2.5 with lag and moving-average features; boosting outperformed LSTM. Supports
**XGBoost** and our feature design.

**[L9] Domalatov et al. (2025), Almaty, Kazakhstan — *International Journal of Sustainable Development and Planning* 20(12), 5227–5246.**
*Data:* PM2.5 and PM10 from 71 Almaty stations (AQICN, AirKaz, air.org.kz), 2020–2024, aggregated to daily
city medians; meteorology (temperature, humidity, wind, boundary-layer height, pressure, cloud cover) from ERA5
and Ogimet. *Task:* forecasting 7 and 30 days ahead on a chronological hold-out. *Models:* Random Forest, LSTM;
persistence and seasonal-naive baselines. Two scenarios: A = pollutant lags only, B = pollutant lags **plus
meteorology**.
*Result:* for PM2.5 at the 7-day horizon, **adding weather reduced Random Forest RMSE from 6.22 to 3.96 µg/m³
and MAE from 4.95 to 3.30 µg/m³**; LSTM improved less (RMSE 7.61 → 6.49). **Random Forest was best for
PM2.5** in every PM2.5 setting. The baseline RMSE for PM2.5 at 7 days was 6.40.
*Where to look:* **Table 3** (RMSE, MAE, MAPE for RF and LSTM, scenarios A/B, 7 and 30 days) and **Table 4**
(baseline comparison). Note: Table 4 repeats some Table 3 values with small inconsistencies (e.g. RF B
PM2.5 30-day 6.91 vs 5.70); we cite Table 3.
*Meaning for us:* the most recent study from Kazakhstan and the strongest evidence that **meteorological
inputs** are the main source of improvement for PM2.5 forecasts; supports adding weather features and keeping
Random Forest.

### B. Estimation studies (same-time inputs) — useful for context, not directly comparable

**[L2] Agibayeva et al. (2022), Astana, Kazakhstan — *Sustainability* 14(24), 16641.**
*Data:* two Kazhydromet stations, 2019, daily means. *Inputs:* concurrent PM10, SO2, CO, NO2, NO and weather.
*Models:* multiple linear regression (MLR) and Random Forest; 80/20 split with 10-fold CV.
*Result:* **Random Forest performed better**, with R² between 0.79 and 0.98; MLR gave R² = 0.84 (heating),
0.68 (non-heating) and 0.99 (combined).
*Where to look:* Section 2.4 (split and CV); Section 3.4 and **Table 5** (MLR); Section 3.5 and **Table 6**
(Random Forest); Abstract for the RF range.
*Meaning for us:* the only verified ML study for Astana; motivates the heating-season analysis and the
**Random Forest** choice. Not a forecast (same-day inputs).

**[L10] Haseeb et al. (2026), Lahore, Pakistan — *Atmosphere* 17(4), 411.**
*Data:* satellite (MODIS, Sentinel-5P), ERA5 reanalysis and one ground monitor, 2019–2024; independent
2024 test year. *Models:* RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost and a weighted ensemble.
*Result:* among single models Random Forest was best (R² = 0.767, RMSE = 24.75), then XGBoost (R² = 0.76,
RMSE = 26.32), CatBoost (R² = 0.73) and LightGBM (R² = 0.70); a **weighted ensemble of RF, XGBoost and CatBoost
was best overall** (R² = 0.7728, RMSE = 23.37; MAE = 17.29).
*Where to look:* Sections 3.2.1–3.2.5 and 3.3 with **Table 2** ("Independent validation performance … using
the 2024 dataset"); MAE only in Section 5 (Conclusions). In Section 4.3 the authors state the model cannot be
used alone to predict future concentrations, because it relies on concurrent pollutant inputs. LightGBM and
CatBoost values are in the same Table 2 and in the Abstract.
*Meaning for us:* RF/XGBoost beat LightGBM/CatBoost, and combining models helped — the basis for our
**ensemble (Model 5)**; also shows why concurrent inputs must not be used for forecasting.

**[L12] Makhdoomi, Sarkhosh & Ziaei (2025), Mashhad, Iran — *Scientific Reports* 15, 8076.**
*Data:* 2,203 matched observations, 2016–2022; random 80/20 split; inputs include concurrent variables.
*Models:* LightGBM, XGBoost, RF, Gradient Boosting Regression (GBR).
*Result:* GBR R² = 0.9802 (RMSE 2.31), XGBoost R² = 0.9781, RF R² = 0.9686 (MAE 0.47).
*Where to look:* **Table 1** (model comparison) in the full-text PDF.
*Meaning for us:* a cautionary example — near-perfect R² from same-time inputs and a random split is not
comparable with a genuine next-day forecast.

---

## 2.3. Traditional regression methods

Linear models appear as a reference in almost every study. They were competitive in Astana (MLR R² up to
0.99 with concurrent inputs; L2) and were one of the enhanced models in the Albanian day-ahead benchmark
(L6). Their weakness is the inability to model interactions such as "the same recent level means something
different in winter than in summer". **Ridge regression** (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970) adds an L2 penalty that
stabilizes coefficients when many lag and rolling features are correlated — exactly our situation.

## 2.4. Tree-based ensemble models

Tree ensembles were the most frequent winners among forecasting studies: XGBoost in Prishtina (L3) and
Dallas (L5), Gradient Boosting in Bangkok (L8), HistGradientBoosting in Albania (L6); Random Forest was best
in Astana (L2) and the strongest single model in Lahore (L10). **Random Forest** (Breiman, 2001) averages
many decorrelated trees; **XGBoost** (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) adds trees sequentially with regularization. On
daily data both beat LSTM where compared (L5, L8).

## 2.5. Support vector regression

SVR was the most consistently best model for next-day PM2.5 in Greece (L4) and the best PM2.5 model one hour
ahead in Abu Dhabi (L7). Its ε-insensitive loss ignores small errors and the RBF kernel captures smooth
non-linear effects (Smola & Schölkopf, 2004). It needs feature scaling and is efficient for datasets of our
size (~1,800 days).

## 2.6. Time-series forecasting methods

Lags and rolling statistics of PM2.5 were the core features in every forecasting study (L1, L4, L5, L6, L8),
usually with sine/cosine calendar encoding. Feature importance repeatedly shows recent PM2.5 and short
rolling means as dominant (L1: current value ≈0.72 and rolling mean ≈0.24 of Random Forest importance). The
strongest designs fix chronological boundaries before processing (L4), hold out whole years (L5, L7, L10) or
use rolling-origin backtesting (L6), and include a persistence baseline (L1, L4, L6).

## 2.7. Data sources and dataset limitations

| Data type | Studies | Strength | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenWeather API | L1 | free, global, consistent, programmatic | modelled values for a coordinate; production method not documented (OpenWeather, n.d.) |
| Open modelled fields (CAMS/Open-Meteo) | L6 | reproducible, multi-city | model output, not measurements |
| Ground stations | L2, L4, L7, L8, L9, L12 | direct measurements | point coverage, gaps |
| Satellite / reanalysis (ERA5) | L5, L9 (weather), L10 | spatial coverage; complete weather records | coarse; reanalysis is not a forecast |

| ID | Study | Task | Horizon | Best model | Reported result | Where to look | Comparable with ours? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | Sapakova 2026 (Almaty) | forecasting | 15–60 min | **Persistence** | R² 0.980 vs ML 0.962–0.977 (15 min) | §3.5, Table 7, Fig. 9 | partly (same API, very short horizon) |
| L3 | Fetahi 2025 (Prishtina) | forecasting | 1 h, 24 h | **XGBoost** | R² 0.862, MAE 3.524 (1 h); R² 0.50 (24 h) | Abstract | partly |
| L4 | Psomadakis 2026 (Greece) | forecasting | **next day** | **SVM** | 13/20 wins; all ML > persistence | Abstract, §6.1, Table 8, Fig. 9, §8 | **yes, closest** |
| L5 | Chivukula 2026 (USA) | forecasting | **next day** | **XGBoost** | R² 0.667 (RF 0.588, LSTM 0.555) | §3.6, Table 6 | **yes** |
| L6 | Hyso 2026 (Albania) | forecasting | **1–3 days** | **HistGBM** | MAE 1.92 vs 2.04 baseline | Table 4, p. 631 | **yes** |
| L7 | Abuouelezz 2025 (UAE) | forecasting | 1 h – 1 week | **Linear SVR** (1 h) | MAE 6.630, RMSE 15.911 | Table 5 | partly |
| L8 | Bhatta 2026 (Bangkok) | forecasting | 1–7 days | **Gradient Boosting** | RMSE 2.17 | Abstract | partly |
| L9 | Domalatov 2025 (Almaty) | forecasting | 7 and 30 days | **Random Forest + weather** | RMSE 6.22 → 3.96 with meteorology | Table 3 | partly (daily, Kazakhstan, longer horizon) |
| L2 | Agibayeva 2022 (Astana) | estimation | none | **Random Forest** | R² 0.79–0.98 | §3.5, Table 6 | no |
| L10 | Haseeb 2026 (Lahore) | estimation | none | **Ensemble (RF/XGB/CatBoost)** | R² 0.7728 (RF 0.767 > XGB 0.76 > CatBoost 0.73 > LightGBM 0.70) | §3.3, Table 2 | no |
| L12 | Makhdoomi 2025 (Mashhad) | estimation | none | **GBR** | R² 0.9802 | Table 1 | no |

**What the comparison shows.** In the five studies that are closest to our task (L4, L5, L6, L7, L8 —
future forecasting, daily or near-daily), the winners are **SVM/SVR** (L4, L7) and **gradient-boosted
trees** (L5, L6, L8). Random Forest is consistently close behind and was best in the Astana estimation study
(L2). Linear models are weaker but remain a meaningful reference (L6). LSTM never won on daily data (L5, L8).
Persistence is strong at very short horizons (L1) and must always be reported (L4, L6). The very high scores
of L2, L10 and L12 come from estimation designs and are not comparable with ours. Finally, the Almaty study
by Domalatov et al. (L9) shows that the largest single improvement comes not from changing the algorithm but from
**adding meteorological information** (−36% RMSE for Random Forest).

## 2.9. Strengths and limitations of the literature

* Short-horizon results (L1, L3, L7) overstate what is possible for a day-ahead daily mean.
* Concurrent inputs (L2, L10, L12) and random splits (L2, L12) inflate accuracy.
* Reporting is inconsistent: some studies give only R² (L4, L5), others only MAE/sMAPE (L6).
* Central Asian evidence is limited to Almaty (L1 nowcasting, L9 7–30-day forecasting) and Astana estimation (L2); none forecasts the next-day mean for Astana.
* Modelled API data (L1, L6) were not validated against ground stations in those studies.

## 2.10. Model selection derived from the literature

**Table 2.2.** From evidence to the models we train.

| Model family | Evidence in similar studies | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| **Support Vector Regression (RBF)** | best next-day model in Greece (L4: 13/20 wins); best 1-h model in UAE (L7) | **Selected** (Model 4) |
| **Gradient-boosted trees** | best in Dallas next-day (L5: XGBoost R² 0.667), Albania day-ahead (L6: HistGBM), Bangkok (L8), Prishtina (L3) | **Selected as XGBoost** (Model 3) |
| **Random Forest** | best in Almaty with weather (L9), Astana (L2), best single model in L10, second in L5 | **Selected** (Model 2) |
| **Regularized linear regression** | competitive reference in L6 (Ridge) and L2 (MLR) | **Selected as Ridge** (Model 1) — interpretable baseline model |
| **Persistence** | beats ML at 15 min in Almaty (L1); minimum bar in L4 and L6 | **Selected as non-ML baseline** |
| LSTM / deep learning | never best on daily data (L5: R² 0.555 < XGBoost 0.667; L8); needs more data than our ~1,800 days | **Not selected** |
| SARIMA | worse than persistence at most stations (L4) | **Not selected** |
| **Ensemble of the best models** | weighted RF+XGBoost+CatBoost ensemble best in L10 | **Selected as Model 5**: equal-weight average of tuned RF + XGBoost + SVR |
| **Meteorological inputs** | RF RMSE −36% with weather (L9); weather drives episodes (L8, L10) | **Added**: Open-Meteo past weather + target-day weather (configs `full_weather`, `full_weather_past`) |
| LightGBM / CatBoost | below RF and XGBoost in L10 (R² 0.70 / 0.73); HistGBM competitive in L6 | **Not selected** — same family as XGBoost, no evidence of a gain |

**Feature and evaluation decisions taken from the same studies:**

* lags, rolling means/SD and cyclical calendar features (L1, L4, L5, L6, L8);
* only information available before the forecast time — no concurrent co-pollutants (lesson from L10, L12);
* year-based split: train / validation year / independent test year (L5, L7, L10);
* persistence baseline on identical dates (L1, L4, L6);
* separate evaluation of high-pollution days and the heating season (L2, L10);
* MAE as the primary metric plus RMSE, R² and sMAPE, because studies report different metrics (L4, L6);
* meteorological features from a reanalysis archive for training and a weather forecast for live use (L9).

## 2.11. Research gap

The verified Kazakh studies address same-day estimation in Astana with station data (L2), 15-minute
nowcasting in Almaty with OpenWeather data (L1), or 7–30-day forecasting in Almaty with station and ERA5 data
(L9). We did not find a study that evaluates a
**day-ahead daily-mean** PM2.5 forecast for **Astana** using **multi-year OpenWeather historical data**,
leakage-free issue-time features, a year-based train/validation/test design and an explicit persistence
baseline. This project addresses that gap; we do not claim that no similar work exists elsewhere.

## 3. Materials and Methods

### 3.1. Dataset provenance

Data were obtained from the OpenWeatherMap Air Pollution API history endpoint (OpenWeather, n.d.) for the
coordinate 51.1694 N, 71.4491 E (Astana) using 0 API requests in 7-day chunks with adaptive
splitting, retry/backoff and a resumable manifest. The values are API-provided concentrations for a coordinate;
they are not readings from a specific ground monitor and were not validated against stations in this project.

### 3.2. Dataset size, variables and quality

The raw dataset contains 43,273 hourly records covering 2020-12-26T00:00 to 2025-12-31T23:00 (local). Timestamp coverage is 98.42%
(696 missing hours; 20 gaps, longest 120 h, 6 longer than 24 h); 0 duplicated timestamps were found in the raw file;
1,783 of 1,832 local days have at least 20 valid hours; hourly PM2.5 ranges over 0.00–87.67 µg/m³. Variables: CO,
NO, NO2, O3, SO2, PM2.5, PM10, NH3 (all µg/m³) and the provider AQI (1–5). See `docs/data_dictionary.md`.

### 3.3. Cleaning

Schema validation, removal of invalid/future timestamps, chronological sorting, duplicate removal, invalidation of
negative concentrations and out-of-range AQI, reindexing to a complete hourly grid without interpolation, and
flagging (not removing) statistical extremes. These operations are split-independent. Imputation, scaling and
feature selection are fitted on training data only, inside scikit-learn pipelines.

### 3.4. Target definition and forecasting protocol

A forecast is issued at 18:00 Asia/Almaty on day *d*. The target is the mean of all valid hourly PM2.5 records of
local day *d*+1, retained only when at least 20 hours are valid. Records are labelled by the start of their hour;
the newest usable record at 18:00 is labelled 17:00. Leakage is excluded by construction and verified by
automated tests that overwrite all future observations and confirm that no feature changes.

### 3.5. Feature engineering, normalization and feature selection

Three nested feature configurations were built: *basic* (target-day calendar features + last PM2.5; 10
features), *lag* (+ PM2.5 lags at 24/48/72 h and recent values/24-h lags of the other pollutants; 24 features)
and *full* (+ trailing means over 6–72 h, 24-h standard deviation, minimum, maximum and trend, previous-day mean,
PM2.5/PM10 ratio and 24-h means of all pollutants; 43 features). The *full_selected* configuration adds an
in-pipeline selector (variance threshold → correlation-redundancy filter → top-*k* by F-statistic, with *k*
tuned). Historical AQI was tested only as an ablation (*full_aqi*). Following Domalatov et al. (2025), meteorological
features from Open-Meteo (Zippenfenig, 2023) were added: past-24-hour weather before the issue time (strictly
leakage-free; *full_weather_past*) and target-day weather (*full_weather*). In the historical benchmark the
target-day weather comes from reanalysis ("perfect prognosis"), whereas live forecasts use the Open-Meteo weather
forecast; *full_weather* therefore gives an optimistic estimate and *full_weather_past* the strict one.
StandardScaler is applied for Ridge and SVR.

### 3.6. Data partitions

Samples are assigned by target date: train 2021–2023, validation 2024, test 2025 (train 1061, validation 351, test 346 eligible
samples). The same eligible dates are used for every model and for persistence.

**Table 3.** Distribution of the daily target in each partition (µg/m³).

| split | count | mean | std | 50% | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| test | 346.00 | 5.11 | 6.09 | 2.76 | 40.06 |
| train | 1061.00 | 6.24 | 5.72 | 4.47 | 46.21 |
| unused | 5.00 | 8.11 | 5.69 | 5.39 | 15.04 |
| validation | 351.00 | 5.92 | 6.38 | 3.42 | 34.23 |

### 3.7. Models and hyperparameter optimization

Ridge Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and RBF-kernel SVR were tuned with RandomizedSearchCV (25 candidates,
seed 42) on the training years using TimeSeriesSplit (5 folds, 1-day gap) and MAE scoring. The model and feature
configuration with the lowest 2024 validation MAE was selected; each model's selected configuration was refitted
on 2021–2024 and evaluated once on 2025. Model 5 is the equal-weight average of the tuned Random Forest, XGBoost and SVR (motivated by
Haseeb et al., 2026). The persistence baseline repeats the trailing 24-hour mean available at 18:00.

### 3.8. Mathematical formulations

All formulas are written in LaTeX (copy into Word via *Insert → Equation → LaTeX*, or into any LaTeX editor).
Each formula matches the implemented code; the "Code" line gives the function that computes it.

**Notation.** $h$ indexes hourly records labelled by the **start** of their hour (OpenWeatherMap `dt`).
$x^{(p)}_h$ is the API-provided concentration of pollutant $p$ (µg/m³) in hour $h$. $d$ is a local calendar date
(Asia/Almaty). The issue time for date $d$ is $\tau_d = d\;18{:}00$ local. A record labelled $h$ is available at
time $h + 1\,\mathrm{h}$; the set of records usable at $\tau_d$ is therefore $\{h : h + 1\,\mathrm{h} \le \tau_d\}$,
and the newest usable record is $h^{*}_d = \tau_d - 1\,\mathrm{h}$ (17:00).

---

## 1. Next-day PM2.5 target

$$
y_d \;=\; \bar{x}^{(\mathrm{PM2.5})}_{d+1}
\qquad\text{(defined only if } |H_{d+1}| \ge N_{\min}\text{)}
$$

* $y_d$: target for a forecast issued at $\tau_d$; $N_{\min}=20$ (configurable `forecast.target_min_valid_hours`).
* **Why:** a genuine day-ahead quantity: nothing from day $d+1$ is known at $\tau_d$.
* **Code:** `feature_engineering.daily_targets`, `build_dataset`.

## 2. Daily average aggregation

$$
\bar{x}^{(\mathrm{PM2.5})}_{D} \;=\; \frac{1}{|H_D|}\sum_{h \in H_D} x^{(\mathrm{PM2.5})}_h ,
\qquad H_D = \{h : \mathrm{date}_{\mathrm{local}}(h) = D,\; x^{(\mathrm{PM2.5})}_h \text{ observed}\}
$$

* $|H_D|$ is the number of valid hourly observations on local date $D$ (usually 24; 25 on 2024-02-29 when
  Kazakhstan moved from UTC+6 to UTC+5). Stored as `target_valid_hours`.
* **Code:** `feature_engineering.daily_targets`.

## 3. Missing-value handling

Missing hours are **not** interpolated. A windowed statistic is computed only when the share of valid hours
reaches a coverage threshold $c$ (= 0.75, `forecast.rolling_min_coverage`); otherwise the feature is missing.
Missing feature values are then imputed inside each model pipeline with the training-fold median:

$$
\tilde{z}_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
z_{ij}, & z_{ij} \text{ observed} \\
\operatorname{median}\{z_{kj} : k \in \mathcal{T},\; z_{kj} \text{ observed}\}, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

* $\mathcal{T}$: indices of the **training** samples of the current fold. Targets are never imputed.
* **Code:** `feature_engineering._cov_ok`; `sklearn.impute.SimpleImputer(strategy="median")` in `models.build_pipeline`.

## 4. Standardization (Ridge and SVR only)

$$
z'_{ij} = \frac{\tilde{z}_{ij} - \mu_j}{\sigma_j},
\qquad \mu_j = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}} \tilde{z}_{kj},
\quad \sigma_j = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}} (\tilde{z}_{kj}-\mu_j)^2}
$$

* $\mu_j,\sigma_j$ are estimated on the training fold only and reused for validation/test rows.
* **Code:** `sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` in `models.build_pipeline`.

## 5. Lag features

$$
\mathrm{lag}^{(p)}_{L}(d) = x^{(p)}_{\,h^{*}_d - L}, \qquad L \in \{24, 48, 72\}\ \text{hours}
$$

and the last available value $\mathrm{last}^{(p)}(d) = x^{(p)}_{h^{*}_d - a}$ with the smallest age
$a \in \{0,1,2\}$ for which the record is observed (`last_value_max_age_hours` = 3).

* **Code:** `feature_engineering.compute_features` (`at`, `_last_valid`).

## 6. Rolling means

$$
\mathrm{mean}^{(p)}_{w}(d) = \frac{1}{|V_w|}\sum_{h \in V_w} x^{(p)}_h,
\qquad V_w = \{h : h^{*}_d - w < h \le h^{*}_d,\; x^{(p)}_h \text{ observed}\},
\qquad \text{if } \tfrac{|V_w|}{w} \ge c
$$

* $w \in \{6,12,24,48,72\}$ h for PM2.5; $w=24$ h for the other pollutants. Every window ends at $h^{*}_d$, i.e.
  strictly before the issue time.
* **Code:** `feature_engineering._mean`.

## 7. Rolling standard deviation (and min/max, trend)

$$
\mathrm{sd}_{24}(d) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|V_{24}|-1}\sum_{h \in V_{24}} \left(x_h - \mathrm{mean}_{24}(d)\right)^2}
$$

Trend: ordinary-least-squares slope of PM2.5 against hour index $t$ over the last 24 h,
$\beta_{24}(d) = \dfrac{\sum (t - \bar t)(x_t - \bar x)}{\sum (t-\bar t)^2}$ (µg/m³ per hour).

* **Code:** `feature_engineering._std`, `_min`, `_max`, `_slope`.

## 8. Ridge Regression

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\beta_0,\boldsymbol\beta}\;
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \mathbf{z}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta\right)^2 + \alpha\,\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2 ,
\qquad \hat{y} = \hat\beta_0 + \mathbf{z}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
$$

* $\alpha > 0$ controls L2 shrinkage (tuned on a log scale in $[10^{-3},10^{3}]$). Closed form:
  $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (Z^{\top}Z + \alpha I)^{-1} Z^{\top}\mathbf{y}$ for centred data.
* **Why:** stable coefficients under the strong collinearity of lag/rolling features (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970).
* **Code:** `models.make_estimator("ridge")`.

## 9. Random Forest prediction aggregation

$$
\hat{y}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(\mathbf{z};\,\Theta_b)
$$

* $T_b$: regression tree grown on a bootstrap sample (drawn with replacement) of the training data, with a random
  subset of `max_features` candidate features at each split; each leaf predicts the mean target of its samples;
  splits minimise the within-node squared error. $B$ = `n_estimators` (Breiman, 2001).
* **Code:** `models.make_estimator("random_forest")`.

## 10. XGBoost additive boosting

$$
\hat{y}^{(K)}_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \eta\, f_k(\mathbf{z}_i),
\qquad
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^2 + \sum_{k=1}^{K}\Omega(f_k),
\qquad
\Omega(f) = \gamma T + \tfrac{1}{2}\lambda \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert_2^2
$$

At iteration $k$ the new tree minimises the second-order approximation
$\sum_i \left[g_i f_k(\mathbf{z}_i) + \tfrac12 h_i f_k(\mathbf{z}_i)^2\right] + \Omega(f_k)$ with
$g_i = \partial_{\hat y}\ell$, $h_i = \partial^2_{\hat y}\ell$; the optimal leaf weight is
$w_j^{*} = -\dfrac{\sum_{i\in I_j} g_i}{\sum_{i\in I_j} h_i + \lambda}$.

* $\eta$ = `learning_rate`, $T$ = number of leaves, $\lambda$ = `reg_lambda`, $\mathbf{w}$ = leaf weights
  (Chen & Guestrin, 2016). The base score (initial prediction) is omitted for brevity.
* **Code:** `models.make_estimator("xgboost")` (objective `reg:squarederror`).

## 11. SVR ε-insensitive loss

$$
\min_{\mathbf{w},b,\boldsymbol\xi,\boldsymbol\xi^{*}}\;
\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\xi_i + \xi_i^{*})
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\begin{cases}
y_i - \mathbf{w}^{\top}\phi(\mathbf{z}_i) - b \le \varepsilon + \xi_i\\
\mathbf{w}^{\top}\phi(\mathbf{z}_i) + b - y_i \le \varepsilon + \xi_i^{*}\\
\xi_i,\xi_i^{*} \ge 0
\end{cases}
$$

Equivalently the loss is $\ell_\varepsilon(r) = \max(0, |r| - \varepsilon)$. Prediction:
$\hat y(\mathbf{z}) = \sum_i (\alpha_i - \alpha_i^{*}) K(\mathbf{z}_i,\mathbf{z}) + b$ with the RBF kernel
$K(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}') = \exp(-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}'\rVert^2)$ (Smola & Schölkopf, 2004).

* $C$: regularization trade-off; $\varepsilon$: width of the no-penalty tube (µg/m³); $\gamma$: kernel bandwidth.
* **Code:** `models.make_estimator("svr")`.

## 12. MAE

$$\mathrm{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert y_i - \hat y_i \rvert \quad [\mu g/m^3]$$

**Code:** `evaluation.mae` (primary model-selection metric).

## 13. RMSE

$$\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat y_i)^2} \quad [\mu g/m^3]$$

**Code:** `evaluation.rmse`.

## 14. Coefficient of determination

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2}$$

$\bar y$ is the mean of the evaluated targets. $R^2$ can be negative and is **not** a percentage of correct
predictions. **Code:** `evaluation.r2`.

## 15. sMAPE (and guarded MAPE)

$$
\mathrm{sMAPE} = \frac{100\%}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{2\,\lvert y_i-\hat y_i\rvert}{\lvert y_i\rvert+\lvert\hat y_i\rvert+\epsilon},
\qquad
\mathrm{MAPE}_{\ge 1} = \frac{100\%}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}\frac{\lvert y_i-\hat y_i\rvert}{\lvert y_i\rvert},\;
S=\{i: \lvert y_i\rvert \ge 1\,\mu g/m^3\}
$$

$\epsilon = 10^{-6}$. MAPE is restricted to targets ≥ 1 µg/m³ because it explodes near zero.
**Code:** `evaluation.smape`, `evaluation.mape`.

## 16. Persistence baseline

$$\hat y^{\mathrm{pers}}_d = \mathrm{mean}^{(\mathrm{PM2.5})}_{24}(d) = \frac{1}{|V_{24}|}\sum_{h=h^{*}_d-23}^{h^{*}_d} x^{(\mathrm{PM2.5})}_h$$

The trailing 24-h mean ending at 17:00 on day $d$ — fully available at 18:00 (unlike the calendar-day mean of $d$).
**Code:** `models.PersistenceForecaster`.

## 17. Relative improvement against persistence

$$
S_{\mathrm{MAE}} = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{model}}}{\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{pers}}},
\qquad \Delta_{\%} = 100\, S_{\mathrm{MAE}}
$$

$S>0$: the model beats persistence on the same dates; $S<0$: persistence is better.
**Code:** `evaluation.skill_vs_persistence`, column `test_mae_improvement_pct` in `model_comparison.csv`.

## 18. Empirical prediction interval (optional output)

$$
\left[\hat y + q_{0.05}(r),\; \hat y + q_{0.95}(r)\right],\qquad r = y - \hat y \text{ on the 2024 validation year}
$$

Residuals $r$ come from the train-only fit; the interval is approximate (assumes residuals in operation resemble
validation residuals) and is clipped at 0. **Code:** `training._bundle`, `prediction.make_forecast`.

### 3.9. Evaluation metrics and experimental design

MAE (primary), RMSE, R², sMAPE, MAPE (targets ≥ 1 µg/m³), bias and skill relative to persistence. Experiments:
E1 model comparison; E2 feature engineering; E3 feature selection; E4 default vs tuned; E5 elevated-pollution
days (training 90th percentile and WHO 15 µg/m³); E6 interpretability; E7 robustness across months, seasons
and heating periods.

## 4. Results and Discussion

### 4.1. Exploratory analysis

Mean hourly PM2.5 by season: Winter 8.42, Spring 6.09, Summer 3.21, Autumn 6.15 µg/m³; 7.85 µg/m³ in the heating season vs 4.06 µg/m³ outside it (Fig. 4). Daily means show strong persistence
(lag-1 daily autocorrelation 0.591, lag-7 0.183; Fig. 6). The WHO 24-hour guideline of 15 µg/m³ was exceeded on 143 of 1782 valid days (Fig. 3b). Figures 1–7
are in `artifacts/figures/`.

### 4.8. Evaluation of hypotheses

* **H1 (RQ1):** Not supported: the lowest 2024 validation MAE was obtained by Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) (full_weather, 2.227 µg/m³).
* **H2 (RQ2):** Supported: engineered features (best of lag/full) lowered validation MAE for 3 of 5 models (basic → engineered: Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) 3.105→3.091; Random Forest 3.116→3.118; Ridge Regression 3.405→3.225; SVR (RBF) 3.155→3.080; XGBoost 3.156→3.163).
* **H3 (RQ3):** Supported: on the 2025 test the selected Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) obtained MAE 3.015 µg/m³ vs 3.516 µg/m³ for persistence (skill +0.142, i.e. +14.2% MAE change); 4 of 5 ML models beat persistence.
* **H4 (RQ4):** Not supported: the three most important features of Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) by test-set permutation importance were pm25_last, pm10_last, target_month_cos (1 of 3 are PM2.5-history features). Importance is associational, not causal.
* **H5 (RQ5):** Supported: on 33 elevated test days (> 13.2 µg/m³, training 90th percentile) the MAE of Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) was 9.937 vs 2.285 µg/m³ on other days (ratio 4.35); bias on elevated days -9.547 µg/m³.

### 4.9. Discussion

*Benchmark run of 17 November 2026 with five models and seven feature configurations
(`artifacts/metrics/`). All numbers below are read from `model_comparison.csv`, `all_results.csv`,
`E5_elevated_pollution.csv`, `E6_summary.json` and `E7_heating_errors.csv`.*

**Data.** 43,273 hourly OpenWeatherMap records (26 Dec 2020 – 31 Dec 2025 local; 98.4% timestamp coverage,
no duplicates) and hourly Open-Meteo weather for the same period. After eligibility filtering: 1,061 training
(2021–2023), 351 validation (2024) and 346 test (2025) daily samples. Mean hourly PM2.5 was 7.85 µg/m³ in the
heating season and 4.06 µg/m³ outside it; the 2025 test year was cleaner than the training years (median daily
target 2.76 vs 4.47 µg/m³; KS p < 0.001).

**Model selection (validation 2024).** Adding weather produced the largest improvement of the whole study on
the validation year: the best validation MAE fell from 3.070 µg/m³ without weather (Ensemble, *full_selected*)
to **2.227 µg/m³ with weather (Ensemble, *full_weather*)**, a 27% reduction that is consistent with the ~36% RMSE
reduction reported by Domalatov et al. (2025) for Almaty. All five models improved on validation with weather
(e.g. XGBoost 3.122 → 2.249, SVR 3.075 → 2.261, Random Forest 3.094 → 2.352). Following the protocol, the
**Ensemble (equal-weight RF + XGBoost + SVR) with *full_weather*** was selected and frozen.

**Independent test (2025).**

| Model (selected configuration) | Test MAE | Test RMSE | Test R² | Better than persistence (MAE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ensemble, full_weather (selected)** | **3.015** | **4.655** | **0.414** | **14.2%** |
| SVR, full_weather | 2.959 | 4.665 | 0.411 | 15.8% |
| XGBoost, full_weather | 3.148 | 4.768 | 0.385 | 10.5% |
| Random Forest, full_weather | 3.120 | 4.793 | 0.378 | 11.2% |
| Ridge, full_weather | 3.715 | 5.271 | 0.248 | −5.7% |
| Persistence | 3.516 | 6.059 | 0.006 | — |

The large validation gain did **not** transfer fully to 2025. Compared with the best model without weather
in the same run (SVR, *full_selected*: test MAE 2.925, RMSE 5.017, R² 0.319), the selected weather ensemble has
a slightly higher MAE (+0.09 µg/m³) but a clearly lower RMSE (−0.36 µg/m³) and higher R² (0.414 vs 0.319): it
makes fewer large errors and slightly more small ones. The reason is visible in E7: in the non-heating season
the weather models over-predict (bias +1.5 µg/m³ for the ensemble, MAE 1.85 vs 1.48 for persistence), while in
the heating season they are much better than persistence (MAE 4.27 vs 5.70). A plausible explanation is the
cleaner 2025 summer, so the same weather produced less PM2.5 than in 2021–2024. A second is that target-day
weather in training is reanalysis (perfect prognosis). The strictly operational configuration with only past
weather (*full_weather_past*) gave the most stable results: Ensemble test MAE 2.942, Random Forest R² 0.433
(the highest test R² of the study). Test results were not used to change any choice.

**Hypotheses.**
* **H1** (a tree ensemble is best) — *partly supported*: the selected model is the ensemble of Random Forest,
  XGBoost and SVR; among single models with weather, XGBoost had the best validation MAE (2.249).
* **H2** (engineered features help) — *supported*: lag/rolling features lowered validation MAE for every model
  relative to the basic set, and weather features lowered it further for every model.
* **H3** (ML beats persistence) — *supported*: the selected model reduces test MAE by 14.2% (3.516 → 3.015) and
  RMSE by 23% (6.06 → 4.66); four of five models beat persistence (Ridge with weather does not).
* **H4** (recent PM2.5 dominates) — *supported*: top permutation features of the selected model are the last
  PM2.5 value (0.45 µg/m³ MAE increase) and last PM10 (0.26), followed by seasonality and **target-day wind
  speed, number of calm hours, temperature change and pressure change** (0.08–0.11) — the meteorological
  conditions known to trap pollution.
* **H5** (larger errors on episodes) — *supported*, but weather helped: on the 33 test days above the training
  90th percentile (13.2 µg/m³) the selected model's MAE was 9.94 µg/m³ (12.68 for the pollution-only SVR selected in the first run)
  versus 2.29 on other days, with a negative bias of −9.6 µg/m³. For days above the WHO 15 µg/m³ guideline
  (n = 23) the best model was SVR with weather (MAE 10.92), now better than persistence (11.34).

**Interpretation.** Meteorology is the most valuable addition: it improves validation accuracy for every
model, reduces large errors and improves forecasts of pollution episodes, in line with Domalatov et al. (2025).
Year-to-year changes in the relationship between weather and PM2.5 (the clean 2025 summer) limit the
improvement in mean absolute error on the test year, which shows why an independent test year is necessary.
Day-ahead accuracy (R² ≈ 0.41) remains far below concurrent-estimation studies (R² ≈ 0.98; Makhdoomi et al.,
2025), which answer a different question.

**Live demonstration.** On 17 Nov 2026 (before 18:00, `--issue-mode latest`) the system used the selected
ensemble with the Open-Meteo weather forecast and issued 3.32 µg/m³ for 17 Nov 2026 (forecast issued 16 Nov
18:00). The OpenWeatherMap provider forecast for the same day was 3.21 µg/m³ (reference only).

### 4.10. Comparison with the literature

Our results refer to a day-ahead daily mean of API-provided concentrations, so they are compared with studies
of the same horizon only qualitatively. Day-ahead benchmarks that include persistence reported modest gains of
ML over simple references (Hyso & Gjylapi, 2026; Psomadakis et al., 2026), while concurrent-estimation studies
report much higher R² that is not comparable with forecasting (Makhdoomi et al., 2025; Agibayeva et al., 2022).

### 4.11. Practical demonstration

Forecast issued 2026-11-16T18:00:00+05:00 for 2026-11-17: **3.32 µg/m³** (ensemble, data freshness 2026-11-16T17:00:00+05:00, reliable=True)

### 4.12. Limitations

See `docs/limitations.md`: modelled API data without ground validation; single coordinate; no meteorological
forecasts as inputs; one test year; small number of elevated days; operational latency of the API.

---

## 5. Conclusion

1. **RO1.** 43,273 hourly records were downloaded and validated (98.42% timestamp coverage,
   1,783 of 1,832 valid days).
2. **RO2.** PM2.5 is strongly seasonal (7.85 µg/m³ in the heating season vs 4.06 µg/m³ outside it) and persistent (lag-1 daily autocorrelation 0.591, lag-7 0.183).
3. **RO3.** A leakage-free pipeline with an 18:00 issue time was implemented and verified by automated tests.
4. **RO4.** Ridge, Random Forest, XGBoost and SVR were tuned with time-series cross-validation (Table 5).
5. **RO5.** Supported: on the 2025 test the selected Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) obtained MAE 3.015 µg/m³ vs 3.516 µg/m³ for persistence (skill +0.142, i.e. +14.2% MAE change); 4 of 5 ML models beat persistence.
6. **RO6.** Most influential features: pm25_last (0.447), pm10_last (0.256), target_month_cos (0.117), wxf_wind_mean (0.112), wxf_calm_hours (0.096), target_doy_cos (0.094), wxf_temp_change (0.087), wxf_pressure_change (0.085). Elevated days: Supported: on 33 elevated test days (> 13.2 µg/m³, training 90th percentile) the MAE of Ensemble (RF+XGB+SVR) was 9.937 vs 2.285 µg/m³ on other days (ratio 4.35); bias on elevated days -9.547 µg/m³.
7. **RO7.** The command `python -m air_quality.cli predict` produced: Forecast issued 2026-11-16T18:00:00+05:00 for 2026-11-17: **3.32 µg/m³** (ensemble, data freshness 2026-11-16T17:00:00+05:00, reliable=True)
8. **RO8.** The methodology, equations and a verified 11-study literature comparison are documented in `docs/`.

**Recommendations and future work.** Add meteorological forecasts (temperature, wind, boundary-layer
indicators) from a verified source; validate against Kazhydromet ground stations; evaluate rolling-origin
retraining; add a graphical interface (web dashboard) on top of the existing `prediction` module; consider
probabilistic forecasts for exceedance warnings.
